item.title: Chance The Rapper Heads Back To South America For Fugees’ “The Score” Celebration
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Chance The Rapper joins Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean's January anniversary show in Brazil after nearly nine years away.
item.content:encoded:
Chance The Rapper will end a nearly nine-year absence from South American stages by opening for Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean in Brazil.

The Chicago rapper is on the bill for 30 Years of The Score, a one-night concert at Nubank Parque in São Paulo on January 16, 2027.

Chance will share opening duties with Damian “Jr. Gong” Marley and São Paulo rapper Criolo, according to the official event listing.

Hill and Jean are the headliners, and the bill also lists YG Marley and Zion Marley as special guests. General ticket sales opened November 24 for the concert, which is set to start at 9 P.M. local time, with gates opening at 3 P.M.

Chance’s representatives announced his spot on the bill in a November 24 release and pointed to his 2018 appearance at Lollapalooza Argentina. He played the opening day of that festival in the Buenos Aires area alongside acts including Anderson .Paak and the Red Hot Chili Peppers.

Hill and Jean have already performed together in Brazil, closing Global Citizen’s climate programming in Rio de Janeiro. They’ll bring the anniversary show to Brooklyn’s Barclays Center with Clipse on December 17, a month before the São Paulo date.

The Fugees released The Score in 1996, two years after their debut Blunted on Reality. Their second album won Best Rap Album at the 1997 Grammy Awards, and their version of “Killing Me Softly With His Song” won Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals.

Chance also spent 2026 revisiting a Grammy-winning project of his own, taking Coloring Book on a 43-date North American tour for its 10th anniversary.

That mixtape won Best Rap Album in 2017, the same year Chance took Best New Artist and won Best Rap Performance for “No Problem” with Lil Wayne and 2 Chainz. The Recording Industry Association of America certified the mixtape platinum in its anniversary year and certified the Lil Wayne and 2 Chainz collaboration quadruple platinum.

The Coloring Book anniversary also brought a deluxe gold vinyl edition with newly recorded acoustic versions of “Same Drugs,” “Blessings,” and “Summer Friends.”

item.title: Dave Chappelle Blames Leaked Clip For Furor Over Charlie Kirk Joke
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Dave Chappelle takes aim at the leaked Madison Square Garden recording after facing questions about his Charlie Kirk joke.
item.content:encoded:
Dave Chappelle is taking issue with how a clip from his Madison Square Garden act made its way online.

Asked in Washington about the joke he made after Charlie Kirk’s killing, the comedian focused on the person who recorded the set and the people who judged it without hearing the rest.

“I think it remains to be seen what I said,” Chappelle told the Daily Mail in an interview. He argued that posting part of a show without permission and attacking the performance without having been there were the real threat to free speech.

When pressed to explain what the audience heard that the clip didn’t capture, Chappelle replied, “I’m just glad you care about context.”

He didn’t describe what came before or after the joke and called the recording stolen.

Chappelle made the remark about Kirk during a two-night run at Madison Square Garden on November 6 and 7.

The Karmageddon dates were part of the New York Comedy Festival and were phone-free, with guests expected to secure their devices in locked pouches.

In the clip from the New York set, Chappelle shifted from talking about the risks of public speaking to a punch line about how he felt after Kirk’s death.

A second clip from the Garden run captured a separate joke. “I’m sure Charlie Kirk is looking up at us right now, laughing so hard he can’t breathe,” Chappelle said. The line echoes Tony Hinchcliffe’s George Floyd joke from Netflix’s The Roast of Kevin Hart in May: Chappelle swapped in Kirk’s name but kept the setup about looking up from the afterlife and the same punchline. Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, condemned jokes about political assassination in a public statement.

The New York dates weren’t the first time Chappelle included Kirk’s killing in his act. He also discussed the shooting in Dave Chappelle: The Unstoppable…, his December 2025 Netflix special, and had brought up Kirk at the Riyadh Comedy Festival earlier that year.

Kirk was shot and killed while speaking at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, at an event organized by Turning Point USA. Utah prosecutors charged Tyler Robinson with aggravated murder in the shooting and six related offenses.

Judge Tony Graf set jury selection for June 21, 2028, and set aside 105 days for the trial.

After being asked about the reaction to the footage, Chappelle also told the Daily Mail, “People get mad about a lot of things.”

item.title: REI AMI Lands Hosting Deal For ABC’s “Who’s In The Band?”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: REI AMI returns from the London pilot for ABC's contest, where a live vote decides which pop group gets to make an album.
item.content:encoded:
REI AMI will take the microphone when ABC puts five singers in separate booths and asks its judges to build a band.

The rapper hosted the London pilot for “Who’s In The Band?” last year and has now signed on to host the series, according to Deadline.

Deadline first reported that ABC had ordered the show 10 days before it broke the news of her hosting deal. The network plans to air the competition in summer 2027, with Hulu also carrying it in the United States and Disney+ picking it up internationally.

The singers all start on the same song at the same time, but what each judge hears can change from one moment to the next.

Each contestant gets a soundproof booth, and each judge works a mixing desk that lets them listen to one voice apart from the other four. They can cut a contestant while the others are still singing.

By the live finale, viewers will have two groups to choose between: a boy band and a girl band. The winning act gets to make an album with Savan Kotecha, who created the series with Richard Bacon and Simon Cowell. Kotecha, whose songwriting credits include work with One Direction and Ariana Grande, will executive produce the record.

REI AMI knows what it’s like to audition for a single spot in a group.

For Netflix’s animated “KPop Demon Hunters,” the part called for someone who could rap and sing in both English and Korean. She recorded her audition on a $40 microphone in Los Angeles and got the offer three days later.

She got to sing for Zoey, the youngest member of HUNTR/X and the rapper who writes lyrics for the fictional trio.

Ji-young Yoo handled the speaking role, while REI AMI joined EJAE and Audrey Nuna on songs including “Golden.” The three singers later sat down with Jimmy Fallon, who surprised them with a platinum record for the single.

Away from HUNTR/X, REI AMI released her own single, “2LOUD,” through Republic Records in September. It was her first solo release since audiences heard her on the film’s soundtrack.

REI AMI also has more music planned for 2027 alongside her first season as the show’s host.

item.title: Jennifer Lopez Saves Her Vegas Concert Film For A Family Thanksgiving
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Jennifer Lopez wants her family together for her Vegas concert film, just like they were for West Side Story growing up.
item.content:encoded:
Jennifer Lopez had a reason to push back on a summer release for her Las Vegas concert film.

She wanted to watch it with her family on Thanksgiving, the holiday when her mother used to put on West Side Story.

Lopez said in an interview on The Drew Barrymore Show that she asked to save the film for the holiday.

“No can we please just wait till Thanksgiving? I wanna watch it on Thanksgiving with my family,” Lopez recalled telling the people who wanted to put the film out in the summer.

For Lopez the original film was something the family waited a year to see, rather than a movie they could put on whenever they wanted.

It wasn’t only the music that kept Lopez coming back to the film. She told Barrymore that watching Rita Moreno, who shared her Puerto Rican heritage, made her think, “Oh I could do that too.”

Moreno played Anita in the 1961 adaptation and became the first Latina to win an Academy Award when she took home best supporting actress for the part.

Years later, Moreno presented Lopez with the GLAAD Vanguard Award, and Lopez used her acceptance speech to credit Moreno’s performance with building her confidence.

Lopez brings music from that film into The JLO Show: Live in Las Vegas, along with selections from Gypsy and a tribute to Elvis Presley.

She puts those numbers alongside her own records, including “Waiting for Tonight,” “Love Don’t Cost a Thing” and “Jenny From the Block,” with an orchestra, a vocal ensemble and 16 dancers.

The film comes from the last night of her 12-show run at the Colosseum at Caesars Palace, where cameras recorded the March 28 finale.

The concert unfolds in four acts, opening with “I’ll See You in My Dreams” and closing with “Shall We Dance.”

The two-hour cut premieres on CBS on Thursday, November 26, at 8 p.m. Eastern and Pacific, and Paramount+ Premium subscribers can stream the broadcast live through their local CBS station.

A longer version with footage that won’t appear on CBS begins streaming on Thanksgiving at 8 p.m. Eastern for all Paramount+ subscribers.

item.title: T.I. Wants Georgia’s Next Governor To Hear From People Who Get Overlooked
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: T.I. says he wants Georgia's next administration to hear directly from residents who aren't usually heard by people in power.
item.content:encoded:
T.I. wants people who rarely get an audience with Georgia’s leaders to have a say before the next governor takes office.

The Atlanta rapper said his work with Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms’ transition will focus on what people need in their own communities and what the state can do for them.

T.I. explained the assignment in an interview with FOX 5 Atlanta at Jackson Memorial church in northwest Atlanta, where his family held its annual Thanksgiving giveaway.

T.I. said the team wants to know what people in their communities need and “how we can better serve people who probably will go unnoticed and go ignored.” He described his own role in that outreach this way: “I’m just connecting dots, bridging gaps, that’s it.”

That outreach is part of a larger effort Bottoms laid out when she announced her transition team on November 17.

She named staffers to handle the handoff from Gov. Brian Kemp’s administration and seven policy committees to make recommendations for her first budget and legislative agenda.

The staff will also recruit people to serve in the administration, and the transition has opened applications for Georgians interested in state jobs or appointments to boards and commissions.

The main transition committee includes T.I. and Killer Mike. Bottoms said the transition is meant to get her administration ready to act on priorities that include lowering costs and expanding Medicaid, with input from residents and the people who run state agencies.

Both rappers have worked on a transition for Bottoms before, when she went from the Atlanta City Council to the mayor’s office.

They joined her mayoral transition team in 2018, when her agenda included affordable housing, education and tackling corruption at City Hall.

The relationship carried into this year’s governor’s race, when Bottoms appeared on T.I.’s ExpediTIously podcast and discussed their West Atlanta roots.

The two talked about Medicaid and affordable housing, along with her proposal to let Georgians decide whether to legalize marijuana and casino gambling.

Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson on November 3 and is set to be sworn in on January 12 at State Farm Arena in downtown Atlanta as the first Black woman elected governor in the United States.

item.title: 2Pac Leads Three Hip-Hop And R&B Vinyl Picks For Record Store Day Black Friday
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: 2Pac, Rae Sremmurd and Coco Jones bring fresh pressings to indie shops, with online sales waiting until Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
2Pac collectors have a new pressing to look for at independent record shops the morning after Thanksgiving.

Interscope’s 20th-anniversary edition of Pac’s Life arrives Friday, November 27, alongside new vinyl editions from Rae Sremmurd and Coco Jones, according to the Record Store Day Black Friday list.

The Pac’s Life reissue comes on two earth-brown records with new packaging, and Record Store Day lists 4,500 U.S. copies.

It opens with Swizz Beatz’s remix of “Untouchable” featuring Bone Thugs-N-Harmony and puts the title track with T.I. and Ashanti on the same side.

Keyshia Cole and Ludacris appear on separate versions of “Playa Cardz Right,” collaborations that go back to the original posthumous release in November 2006.

Rae Sremmurd’s SremmLife 2 also gets two LPs for its anniversary, but the duo’s expanded edition changes what’s on the records.

The dark indigo pressing, limited to 3,000 copies in the U.S., includes five tracks left off the original vinyl, with “Swang,” “Just Like Us,” “Patti Cake” and “Pole Code” sharing the last side. “Black Beatles” is still there, on side two.

Coco Jones takes a different route with Why Not More? (MORE!), putting the eight deluxe tracks from her debut album on a 2,000-copy U.S. 12-inch EP.

Lady London appears on “Is It Mine,” while Leon Thomas joins the “Here We Go (Uh Oh)” remix and Alicia Keys guests on the “Other Side of Love” remix.

The two anniversary albums are marked RSD First, which means independent stores get the first shot, but other retailers may carry the editions later. Jones’ EP is listed as an RSD Exclusive, meaning the physical release is for independent record stores only.

To shop Friday, start with the organizer’s participating-store directory and look for the P next to a shop’s name.

That marks U.S. stores that have signed the pledge, not stores that are guaranteed to have your pick.

Check opening hours and ask about the specific title before making the trip, since shops choose their own orders and may receive fewer copies than requested.

Amoeba Music, for example, says it’ll sell only one copy of each title per customer and won’t take holds or phone orders.

U.S. shops that sell leftover stock online can’t start until Saturday morning, November 28, and not every store will offer that option.

item.title: Blueface Tells Chrisean Rock To Log Off After Her Kick Plea
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Blueface disputes Chrisean Rock's account of how she's been treated and tells her to consider logging off after her Kick plea.
item.content:encoded:
Blueface disputes the account Chrisean Rock gave her Kick audience about how he’s treated her. He turned the accusation back on Rock when a reporter asked about her complaints.

“She is the bully,” Blueface said in an interview with TMZ at Los Angeles International Airport.

Blueface pushed back on the suggestion that he had something against Rock.

“I’ve dealt with it for a long time. So I know how she is,” he said. Blueface said he would pray for her and pointed to the platforms where the criticism keeps reaching her, adding, “Maybe stay off the social media.”

Blueface was answering complaints Rock made during a November 24 livestream on Kick, where she cried as she talked about attacks on her parenting.

Rock said she kept coming across clips of Blueface putting her down and wanted him to stop. Rock told viewers she felt pressure to appear stronger than she was, adding, “This is my cry out for help.”

The criticism Rock described on Kick went beyond the things she saw people saying about her as a mother.

She also accused Blueface of telling other people not to work with her, and she told viewers she needed to be able to show up for their son. Blueface’s airport remarks pushed back on her account.

Rock had also publicly described feeling disrespected by Adam22, whom she struck at a Wild ‘N Out event earlier in November.

When TMZ asked Blueface about Adam22 speaking to the police, Blueface said he had no problem with him taking that step if he felt he needed to. He also said he wouldn’t have let Rock approach Adam22 had he known what she intended to do.

TMZ also asked about streamer N3on spending time with Nevaeh Akira, another of Blueface’s former partners. Akira has described the relationship as professional, and Blueface sounded skeptical of that explanation without claiming to know what was going on between them.

Blueface said N3on had called him directly to make sure there was no issue between them and that he had given the streamer his approval.

item.title: 6LACK Opens “Vault 6” As Sold-Out Atlanta Show Caps Debut Anniversary
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: 6LACK pulls old songs out of storage on Black Friday and wraps his debut album's 10th anniversary with a sold-out Atlanta show.
item.content:encoded:
6LACK is opening his archive on Black Friday as he takes the last show of his debut album’s anniversary run home to Atlanta.

His Vault 6 EP arrives November 27 through LVRN/Interscope Records, the same day he plays a sold-out show in the Heaven room at The Masquerade.

The new EP draws from songs that didn’t make his previous albums, an Interscope rep told AllHipHop.

Interscope said the EP draws from several points in his career. “Every album cycle, there’s a group of songs that don’t make the cut. We’re fixing that. Songs don’t deserve to be buried,” 6LACK wrote when he announced the EP on X.

He’s teased “Invested” and “Moves” on social media, but the label didn’t include a full track list in its announcement.

The first song out of the archive is “WWYG (Where Would You Go),” which Interscope released November 24.

The track comes with a video directed by Angelica Valente and Pseudo, and the label said the song looks at what it means to show affection without expecting a relationship to be perfect.

While the EP brings older recordings out for the first time, the anniversary shows have put songs from FREE 6LACK back in his set. He played Irving Plaza in New York and the Blue Note in Los Angeles before heading to Atlanta. At the Blue Note, he played “Never Know,” “Rules” and “One Way” with a live band, and brought out AZ Chike for “All That Matters” from this year’s Love Is the New Gangsta.

The Blue Note set also reached past the debut with “Pretty Little Fears,” from East Atlanta Love Letter. The studio recording features J. Cole and earned a Grammy nomination for Best Rap/Sung Performance.

Before the J. Cole collaboration, the 2016 debut put 6LACK up for his first two Grammys, with the record nominated for Best Urban Contemporary Album and “PRBLMS” up for Best Rap/Sung Performance. That album and East Atlanta Love Letter came before his third album Since I Have a Lover, which later picked up its own nomination in the progressive R&B category.

The Masquerade lists the Atlanta show as an all-ages event with doors opening at 7 p.m.

item.title: J. Cole’s $238 Ticket Price At Center Of Baltimore’s Legal War With Vivid Seats
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: J. Cole's Baltimore stop figures in a city lawsuit accusing ticket reseller Vivid Seats of hiding the true price until checkout.
item.content:encoded:
J. Cole tickets are among the examples Baltimore has put before a judge in a fight over concert prices.

City lawyers say a listing for his show at CFG Bank Arena advertised a $156 ticket on Vivid Seats, but the final checkout screen showed $238. The arena listed the July 23 concert as a stop on his first solo headlining tour in five years.

The J. Cole listing was one of four examples in the complaint filed November 23 by Baltimore’s mayor and City Council, The Baltimore Sun reported.

The city’s attorneys singled out the missing explanation for the extra charges, writing, “There is no mention of the purpose of these mandatory fees.”

The examples also include tickets to see BTS, Megan Moroney and Trevor Noah.

The city says some shoppers could encounter a misleading price before they even reached the marketplace.

Its lawyers allege that search ads showed prices customers couldn’t get on the site and that some listings with an apparent single-ticket price required buyers to take at least two seats. They also allege shoppers didn’t see an itemized breakdown of certain service and delivery charges until the last screen.

Baltimore says some of the practices lasted well beyond the start of a federal rule on ticket pricing.

The city’s investigation found alleged problems with fee disclosure through at least April 2026 and with search advertising through at least July, according to its account.

The federal rule, which took effect in May 2025, requires ticket sellers who advertise a price to show the total upfront, including most mandatory charges.

Vivid Seats disputes that its pricing misled shoppers and points to the same rule in its defense.

“Vivid Seats denies these allegations and has presented ‘all-in pricing’ nationwide since the FTC all-in pricing rule took effect in May 2025,” the company told CBS Baltimore. Baltimore brought its case under the city’s own consumer protection ordinance in the Circuit Court for Baltimore City.

Baltimore is asking a circuit judge to stop the challenged practices and impose civil penalties for each violation, along with legal fees and costs.

item.title: Clipse’s “Hell Hath No Fury” Turns 20: How The Duo Rapped Through A Label Fight
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Clipse keep the Re-Up Gang tapes coming while a label fight stalls the album that becomes Hell Hath No Fury in 2006.
item.content:encoded:
Clipse didn’t wait for a record label to give them another release date after “Grindin’.”

By the time Hell Hath No Fury reached stores on November 28, 2006, Pusha T and Malice had already spent part of the four-year gap between albums making a case for themselves on mixtapes.

The wait began with a label change, not a shortage of music. Arista, which released their 2002 debut Lord Willin’, folded into Jive, and the brothers sued to get out of their deal.

The dispute ended in a 2006 settlement, and the album came out through Jive and their own Re-Up Records.

While the case was in court, the duo teamed up with Philadelphia rappers Ab-Liva and Sandman as the Re-Up Gang. DJ Clinton Sparks hosted We Got It 4 Cheap Vol. 2, where the foursome traded verses over records already in rotation.

Pharrell Williams contributed to that tape, and Pusha told AllHipHop that rap had become more about personality than lyricism.

The mixtape series gave its name to the opener of Hell Hath No Fury, which turns 20 on Saturday.

The Neptunes produced the album, but Pusha didn’t remember those sessions as a victory lap. In an interview, Pusha T told GQ: “Angst, anger and ego fueled that album. We were egomaniacs. We felt wronged by the music industry.”

The anger in the opener gave way to a different kind of unease on “Nightmares,” the last track.

Malice said the verses reflected remorse he was already dealing with, even if he hadn’t set out to make a record about regret.

“There was a lot of pain in dealing with that album,” Malice said.

The brothers came back together on Let God Sort Em Out, their first Clipse album since 2009.

Pharrell produced the July 2025 release, which opens with the two mourning their parents on “The Birds Don’t Sing.”

Looking back after the reunion, Pusha told Pharrell in a Vogue conversation that he wrote the 2006 record from a bitter and competitive place and didn’t want to have to prove those points again.

“I can never make [a] Hell Hath No Fury again,” Pusha said.
